approach_variants.name: Glacier Basin Trail to the east notch
approach_variants.notes: Reach the Monte Cristo townsite on foot or by bike from Barlow Pass, then take the Glacier Basin Trail less than a mile. The spire stands on your left above the trail, roughly 2,000 ft above the basin. When it makes sense, leave the trail and start up toward the base of the ridge — a snowfield early in the season, extremely loose talus once it has gone. Snow or talus leads up a narrowing gully to the lower col, steepening as it goes, commonly 35 to 45 degrees, with the final couloir steeper and more exposed than anything below it. Best done early in the year while the gully still holds snow: melted out it is loose scree badly exposed to rockfall and a poor outing in late summer. Fixed stations exist in the gully and parties have used them to bypass melted-out gaps on the way down.
hazards: Serious rockfall in the approach gully once the snow has melted out
Steep, exposed snow in the final couloir — crampons, and a second tool is worth having
Cornices and hanging snow slabs above the left-hand branch of the gully
Moats and a schrund where the gully snow melts back from the rock
Loose rock on the route itself, especially low on each pitch and on the east aspect
approach_variants.baseFinding: There are two cols, and you rope up at the second one. The snow gully out of Glacier Basin delivers you to the lower col, and that is not where the climbing starts. From it, scramble around the south face on very loose talus to the upper, east notch, and belay there: the first pitch climbs the east side of the spire a short way, then downclimbs a 5.5 crack about twenty feet to a ramp. Two things confirm you are in the right gully on the way up. Where it narrows, a branch heads left and up — that one leads to the northwest ramp of Wilmans Peak, a different objective entirely, and it carries cornices and hanging snow slabs; the left branch at the narrowing is the documented wrong turn. And once the gully is melted out, an old mine shaft sits in it with yellow tailings all around, open enough to look down into. Confirm again at the top: this summit is a table-top barely larger than the three-piton anchor on it. A summit you can walk about on is one of the other spires.
